short_description: A textbook that builds one Bayesian model of outcomes given treatment and covariates and reads every causal quantity from its posterior, and compares it with double machine learning in simulations and in the 401(k), LaLonde and NHEFS data.
description:
Ask double machine learning (DML) how much eligibility for a 401(k) plan raised household savings and it returns one number. Ask for the effect at the median household and each question needs a new derivation and a new run. This book builds one probability model for outcomes given treatment and covariates and reads every causal quantity off its posterior draws: the average effect, the effect in each subgroup, the probability of causation, and the decision that follows.
The central idea is an accounting identity. The average effect is an average of fitted contrasts over a population the analyst chooses, so a change of population changes the answer in a way the model states. Under one stable odds ratio the average effect fills a whole range, and the posterior selects the group on which an effect is stable. For DML the book proves an exact decomposition of the error, and that no interval is both uniformly valid and of bounded expected length. It studies regularization induced confounding and the coupled horseshoe posterior that reduces it. In the simulations the book reports, with 200 observations and five strong confounders, the posterior trails DML slightly with 50 covariates, and DML is more accurate with 150 and with 300 covariates; with thirty weak confounders among 150 covariates the order reverses.
Later chapters cover instruments, bounds, difference in differences, causal decisions and a Bayesian model of a merger, whose price effect is identified by the demand parameters and the form of competition. Every exercise has a solution, and the code folder of this repository holds the scripts, including many of those behind the solutions of Appendix D (in `book_scripts/solutions/`), apart from the results that Appendix F lists as quoted or absent. Version 1.0.1 corrects the print layout of two tables. The book is written for statisticians, econometricians and data scientists.

chapters.title: Causal Questions
chapters.summary:
Causal questions are questions about outcomes that were not observed, and this chapter sets up the Bayesian way to answer them. Potential outcomes name what would happen under each treatment, de Finetti's representation theorem turns a judgement of exchangeability into a model with a prior, and ignorability says which part of the model the data can inform. The causal targets are then functionals of one posterior: the average treatment effect, effects for subgroups and quantiles, and individual attributions. The chapter works one example from the posterior predictive imputation of the missing potential outcomes to the decision it supports, separates prediction from decision and policy, and flags interference between units as a limit of the framework. It proves no new theorem; its role is to fix the vocabulary and the logic that the remaining chapters use.

#### From the literature

The chapter presents or builds on the potential outcomes framework (Neyman 1923; Rubin 1974), exchangeability and the representation theorem (de Finetti 1937), ignorability and the propensity score (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983), Bayesian inference for causal effects (Rubin 1978).

chapters.title: Frameworks for Causal Inference
chapters.summary:
This chapter surveys the frameworks of causal inference and shows how they relate. Fisher grounds inference in the randomization of a design, Neyman and Rubin in potential outcomes and an assignment mechanism, Pearl in structural causal models and the do calculus, Robins in nonparametric structural models and efficiency, and Dawid in decision theory without counterfactuals. The econometric tradition adds instruments, differences in differences and structural models. The chapter compares what each framework calls a cause and where each gets identification, then collects the shared estimation toolkit: outcome regression, weighting, doubly robust scores and learners for heterogeneous effects. It also gives overviews of the g methods for time varying treatments, causal discovery and transportability. A reader who wants only the Bayesian development can skip it on a first reading.

chapters.title: Models, Accounting and Randomization
chapters.summary:
The model is the object of inference, and the average treatment effect is an accounting identity: an average of fitted contrasts over a population that the analyst chooses. The chapter develops that view. A statistical model is a family of processes that must be consistent under restriction of the sample, and the average effect is a functional of the fitted model and a covariate law. Noncollapsibility of the odds ratio shows the gap between the model and its accounting even under randomization, and the choice of scale for logistic regression changes what an average means. Randomization makes the assignment ignorable, so the outcome model need not model who assigned the treatment. The Lanarkshire milk experiment shows a case where the assignment was not ignorable and no model of the recorded variables could repair it. The chapter also asks what this view does to double machine learning.

#### From the literature

The chapter presents or builds on the statistical model as a process (McCullagh 2002), noncollapsibility of the odds ratio (Gail, Wieand and Piantadosi 1984; Greenland, Robins and Pearl 1999), the Lanarkshire milk experiment and its critique (Student 1931), randomization and ignorability (Rubin 1978).

#### New results

No new results of this chapter are catalogued.

#### Key terms

chapters.title: Groups, Urns and Information
chapters.summary:
A treatment effect that is stable across populations is an element of a group acting on the baseline, and an average of it only describes the case mix. This chapter works that out with groups, urns and information. One odds ratio supports a whole range of average effects as the case mix changes. A randomized experiment is an urn from which about half the units are drawn, so the finite and infinite forms of exchangeability disagree, and when units are sampled from a population the experiment identifies only the two arm laws. A Haar prior gives exact coverage in a transformation model with known baselines. The information gap, in nats, measures how far the data are from stability on a scale, and the posterior odds of one scale against another move at an exponential rate set by the gaps. Kidney stone data illustrate the choice of scale.

#### From the literature

The chapter presents or builds on exchangeability and urns (de Finetti 1937; Heath and Sudderth 1976), Sanov's theorem (Sanov 1957) and its inverse for Dirichlet priors (Ganesh and O'Connell 1999), error exponents of tests (Hoeffding 1965; Bahadur 1967), the treatment effect as a group action (McCullagh 2002), bounds on the probability of necessity and sufficiency (Tian and Pearl 2000), stable effects on binary outcomes (Battey and Edgar 2026).

#### New results

- [Range of the average effect under a stable odds ratio](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#average_effect_range_under_case_mix) (Proposition 4.3, page 64; proved): With one conditional odds ratio e^psi for every unit, the average risk difference over all possible case mixes fills the interval from 0 to tanh(psi/4), so the same stable effect supports very different averages. New in this book.
- [Separability](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#separability_of_functionals_on_frechet_class) (Theorem 4.8, page 68; proved): The expectation of a function of two potential outcomes is determined by the two arm laws alone exactly when that function is a sum of a function of each outcome. New in this book.
- [Identified estimands are functions of the margins](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#identified_estimands_are_functions_of_the_margins) (Corollary 4.9, page 68; proved): Any functional of the potential outcome distribution that an experiment identifies depends on the data only through the two arm laws. New in this book.
- [Stratified urns and the reversal](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#stratified_urns_and_the_reversal) (Proposition 4.11, page 69; proved): In a stratified randomized experiment the collapsed contrast of arm means is unbiased for the finite population effect for every urn if and only if both arms are allocated in proportion to the stratum sizes. New in this book.
- [The posterior selects the group](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#posterior_selects_the_group) (Theorem 4.19, page 74; proved): The log posterior odds of one effect scale against another, or against the saturated model, move linearly in n at a rate equal to the difference of their information gaps, with a log n term for the difference in the number of parameters. New in this book.
- [Transport of a stable effect across case mixes](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#effect_transport_bound_by_total_variation) (Proposition 4.27, page 80; proved): The average effect on the scale of a group moves between two case mixes by at most the range of the stratum effects times the total variation distance between the mixes. New in this book.

chapters.title: What Double Machine Learning Assumes
chapters.summary:
Double machine learning estimates one effect while flexible learners fit the nuisance functions around it. This chapter states the method and what it assumes. In the partially linear model the estimator is a regression of an outcome residual on a treatment residual, a Neyman orthogonal score makes nuisance errors enter as products, and cross fitting removes overfitting bias. The error of the estimator decomposes exactly into a noise term, a cross term and a bias term built from the two fitting errors, and the main theorem gives root n normal inference when the treatment keeps some variation after adjustment and the product rate condition holds. The partially linear estimand is a variance weighted average of effects, and the denominator of the estimator is not an overlap diagnostic. The 401(k) data serve as the running example, and a list says what DML assumes.

#### From the literature

The chapter presents or builds on the partially linear model and partialling out (Robinson 1988), Neyman orthogonality (Neyman 1959), double machine learning with cross fitting and its main theorem (Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, Demirer, Duflo, Hansen, Newey and Robins 2018), the interactive model and augmented inverse probability weighting (Robins, Rotnitzky and Zhao 1994), the variance weighting of regression adjustment (Angrist 1998; Aronow and Samii 2016), the 401(k) application (Poterba, Venti and Wise 1995).

#### New results

- [Exact error decomposition of the partialling out estimator](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#exact_error_decomposition_of_the_robinson_estimator) (Lemma 5.3, page 96; proved): The error of the partialling out estimator splits exactly, with no approximation, into a noise term, a cross term with mean zero under cross fitting and a bias term built from the two fitting errors, namely their product minus the effect times the squared treatment error. First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026b), Orthogonality is not enough: double machine learning and the Bayesian alternative, working paper.
- [Two channels](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#two_channels_of_the_dml_bias) (Corollary 5.4, page 98; proved): With the fits held fixed the estimator converges to the truth plus a bias fixed by the inner product of the two fitting errors and the squared treatment error. First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026b), Orthogonality is not enough: double machine learning and the Bayesian alternative, working paper.

chapters.title: The Inverse Weighting Lineage
chapters.summary:
Inverse probability weighting has a long lineage, and this chapter follows it from Horvitz and Thompson to the augmented score. Every improvement has moved weight off the weights and onto an outcome model. Weights explode under weak overlap, trimming changes the estimand, and Basu's elephants show that unbiasedness over the design says little about the sample in hand. Double robustness and balancing weights are presented next to Bayesian views of the propensity score and a matching example from care management. The weighting estimator is shown to be a posterior mean under a suitable prior. In the Robins, Ritov and Wasserman example, a prior that ignores the known propensity is badly off, a prior coupled to it matches Horvitz and Thompson, and a hierarchical estimator removes the factor of one over the propensity from the Horvitz Thompson and Hájek variances.

#### From the literature

#### New results

chapters.title: Orthogonality Is Not Enough
chapters.summary:
Orthogonality removes the first order effect of a nuisance error, and this chapter asks what it leaves. The remainder is a signed difference of two channels, which the standard rate condition bounds in absolute value and so cannot see cancel. The chapter states a sharp rate condition, shows when the bound is attained under retained lasso shrinkage, and shows that if the cross channel were negligible beside the own square channel, a hypothesis its measurements do not support, the treatment error would attenuate the estimate toward zero. The reported interval comes from one nuisance fit and omits how the bias varies across fits, and no learner gives an interval of finite expected length that is valid uniformly in overlap. The same anatomy appears in weighting. A posterior over the nuisance pair integrates over the fit, but a Bayesian analysis with the prior on the structural coefficients does far worse than DML. The evidence is mostly simulated, in linear Gaussian designs, with the 401(k), LaLonde and IHDP data as checks.

#### From the literature

The chapter presents or builds on orthogonal scores and cross fitting (Chernozhukov and coauthors 2018), regularization induced confounding (Hahn, Carvalho, Puelz and He 2018), impossibility of finite length uniform intervals under weak identification (Dufour 1997), the lasso and its rates (Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen 2014).

#### New results

- [Sharp rate condition](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#sharp_rate_condition_for_dml) (Theorem 7.1, page 139; proved): The partialling out estimator with cross fitting is asymptotically normal when the root n times the bias term b, built from the two fitting errors, vanishes, under fourth moment conditions on the fitting errors. First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026b), Orthogonality is not enough: double machine learning and the Bayesian alternative, working paper.
- [Alignment under retained shrinkage](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#alignment_of_errors_under_retained_lasso_shrinkage) (Proposition 7.2, page 140; proved): When both regressions are fitted by the lasso with a common penalty and the shrunken fits are kept, the two fitting errors align in the limit, and the cross channel and the squared treatment error are each of the order of the penalty squared times the sparsity. First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026b), Orthogonality is not enough: double machine learning and the Bayesian alternative, working paper.
- [Attenuation representation](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#attenuation_representation) (Theorem 7.5, page 142; conditional on The hypothesis that the cross channel H_n is negligible relative to the own square channel Q_n is assumed, and the book does not show that any fitting method delivers it. The book's own measurements find the ratio not negligible): When the treatment fitting error does not vanish fast enough and the cross channel is negligible, the estimator is the true effect multiplied by a shrinkage factor below one. First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026b), Orthogonality is not enough: double machine learning and the Bayesian alternative, working paper.
- [Cross fitting: the identity that survives](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#cross_fitted_variance_identity) (Proposition 7.7, page 146; proved): The variance of the cross fitted estimator splits exactly into the variance of the bias across random fits, a covariance and the variance of the remainder, so an interval that ignores the first term can undercover. First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026b), Orthogonality is not enough: double machine learning and the Bayesian alternative, working paper.
- [No uniformly valid interval of finite length](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#no_uniformly_valid_interval_of_finite_length) (Proposition 7.8, page 149; proved): For a fixed sample size, no confidence set for the partialling out effect can both have uniform coverage over all treatment variances and have expected length bounded over that class; the proof follows Gleser and Hwang (1987) and Dufour (1997). First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026b), Orthogonality is not enough: double machine learning and the Bayesian alternative, working paper.
- [Complete shrinkage bias](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#complete_shrinkage_bias) (Proposition 7.10, page 152; proved): Shrinking the confounder coefficients entirely to zero and regressing on treatment alone leaves a limiting bias, the omitted variable bias, that grows toward one as the number of confounders grows when they enter both equations with equal coefficients. First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026b), Orthogonality is not enough: double machine learning and the Bayesian alternative, working paper.

chapters.title: The Horseshoe and the Coupled Prior
chapters.summary:
The horseshoe shrinks noise hard and leaves large signals almost untouched, and this chapter uses it for causal regression. Independent shrinkage of confounder coefficients creates regularization induced confounding, because a shrunk coefficient lets the treatment absorb part of the confounding. Coupling the outcome prior to the treatment model through the estimated treatment regression reduces the bias. The chapter reports simulations at 200 observations: with 50 covariates the coupled posterior trails DML slightly on the average effect and also returns every other summary, with 150 and 300 covariates DML is clearly more accurate, and with thirty weak confounders among 150 covariates the order reverses. It also covers shared local scales and instruments, the global scale, comparison with spike and slab priors, nonlinear nuisances, and a horseshoe nuisance estimator inside DML.

#### From the literature

The chapter presents or builds on the horseshoe prior (Carvalho, Polson and Scott 2010), shrink globally and act locally (Polson and Scott 2011), the horseshoe plus estimator (Bhadra, Datta, Polson and Willard 2017), posterior contraction of the horseshoe (van der Pas, Kleijn and van der Vaart 2014), regularization induced confounding (Hahn, Carvalho, Puelz and He 2018), the simulation comparison of DML and hierarchical Bayes (Nareklishvili, Polson and Sokolov 2026a).

#### New results

#### Key terms

chapters.title: Computing the Posterior
chapters.summary:
This chapter takes up the objection that Bayesian computation is too costly. Horseshoe Gibbs samplers were fast in the Gaussian designs of the book, so at that size computation is no reason to prefer DML, while at 300 or 400 covariates DML with a lasso nuisance is cheaper. When the likelihood cannot be evaluated cheaply, a posterior is a map from noise to parameters: a quantile network trained on simulated pairs of parameter and data with the check loss turns uniform noise and a summary of the data into posterior draws. The chapter gives the algorithm, what the network sees through summaries, how to get posteriors of effects from simulated pairs, and why one usually does not learn the horseshoe posterior this way. Diagnostics, including rank statistics, are part of the computation, and a closing table says which engine to use when.

#### From the literature

The chapter presents or builds on noise outsourcing (Kallenberg 2002), quantile regression and the check loss (Koenker and Bassett 1978), simulation based calibration (Talts, Betancourt, Simpson, Vehtari and Gelman 2018), generative Bayesian computation (Polson and Sokolov 2023), Polya Gamma augmentation (Polson, Scott and Windle 2013).

#### New results

chapters.title: Generative Treatment Effects and Joint Potential Outcomes
chapters.summary:
Noise outsourcing represents any conditional law as a map from noise to outcomes. Learning that map for treated and untreated outcomes gives every conditional and quantile effect and every other functional of the two marginal laws, which is what decisions under concave utility need and the average effect does not supply. This chapter presents the generative treatment effect learner, benchmarks it, treats uncertainty for a learned map and deep learning in high dimensions, and covers individualized decisions, heterogeneity with the horseshoe, quantile regression as a likelihood and comparison with conformal prediction. The joint law of the two potential outcomes is a separate question: the marginals bound it without identifying it, optimal transport supplies a canonical coupling, and a copula prior covers the rest. A coverage study checks the bands on the 401(k) data.

chapters.title: Bayesian Nonparametrics for Causal Inference
chapters.summary:
Under ignorability, causal inference is regression of the potential outcomes on the covariates, and Bayesian nonparametrics puts a prior on the whole response surface. This chapter covers Bayesian additive regression trees, Hill's causal BART, the overlap problem that plain BART meets, and Bayesian causal forests, which separate prognosis from effect and put the propensity score into the prior. It reviews posterior contraction for forests, runs a simulation in the spirit of Hill, and treats Gaussian process causal inference. Every effect, average, conditional or on the treated, is read off one fitted surface with its uncertainty attached. The chapter also looks at heterogeneous effects, instruments and sensitivity in these models, the prior as a selector of structure, the role of the propensity score in a Bayesian model, and trees compared with the horseshoe.

chapters.title: Instruments
chapters.summary:
Instruments identify effects under unmeasured confounding at the price of an exclusion restriction, and this chapter develops the Bayesian treatment. It starts from the linear model and the local average treatment effect as an accounting over compliers, then builds Bayesian instrumental variables. With one weak instrument a posterior reports the weakness as a wide interval, whether the prior sits on the reduced form or on the structural model. With twenty weak instruments a diffuse structural prior is confident and wrong, and a shrunk first stage gives intervals that cover the truth by being wide. A horseshoe on the first stage handles many instruments. The chapter also treats unlikely instruments, kernel methods for nonlinear structural functions, with a proposed global local prior, and Mendelian randomization, which turns Fisher's genetic confounder into an instrument.

#### From the literature

The chapter presents or builds on instrumental variables (Wright 1928), the local average treatment effect (Imbens and Angrist 1994; Angrist, Imbens and Rubin 1996), the returns to schooling application (Card 1995), weak instruments (Bound, Jaeger and Baker 1995; Staiger and Stock 1997), Anderson Rubin sets (Anderson and Rubin 1949), Mendelian randomization (Davey Smith and Ebrahim 2003).

chapters.title: Bounds and Sensitivity
chapters.summary:
The probabilities that a treatment was necessary, sufficient, or both depend on the joint law of the potential outcomes, so they are bounded rather than identified. This chapter derives the bounds, shows how combining experimental and observational data narrows them, and gives the Bayesian reading: a posterior over the position inside the bounds gives a court the probability it actually needs. Partially identified posteriors keep a prior dependence that never washes out. The second half turns to unmeasured confounding. Cornfield's inequality, Rosenbaum's sensitivity parameter and the E value say how strong a hidden confounder must be to overturn a result, and a prior on the confounding parameters turns the threshold into a posterior probability that the effect is positive. Benchmarking on the 401(k) data and Lanarkshire numbers illustrate the method.

#### From the literature

chapters.title: Smoking and Lung Cancer
chapters.summary:
Fisher doubted that smoking causes lung cancer, and this chapter asks how a Bayesian should weigh the evidence. Fisher was right that observation cannot exclude every common cause and wrong about which way the evidence pointed. Cornfield's inequality, dose response, the twin studies, the inhalation paradox, the front door criterion and Mendelian randomization each constrain the alternatives, and the chapter says what a Bayesian synthesis would combine, with the assumptions in view. Bradford Hill's considerations are read as prior information. The front door section simulates a population with a hidden genotype, and a computed illustration, with no cohort data, gives the posterior of the effect under stated priors on the strength of a hidden confounder. The chapter is a historical case study as much as a method, and it says plainly where the data cannot decide.

chapters.title: Difference in Differences with the Horseshoe
chapters.summary:
Two way fixed effects estimates a weighted average of cohort by time effects with possibly negative weights, and this chapter replaces it with a model of the cells. The horseshoe difference in differences estimator keeps an unshrunk event time path, puts horseshoe priors on cohort deviations and on departures from parallel trends, and reports every summary, such as the effect on the treated or an event study, as an accounting of the posterior. A simulation studies its behaviour. The application is the castle doctrine laws and homicide: with equal noise in every state the posterior mean is 0.025 with probability 0.76 of a positive effect, and with population weights, which the residuals support, it is 0.079 with probability 0.998, close to the published eight percent. The chapter relates the estimator to synthetic control and states the assumptions it needs, among them parallel trends after the modelled departures and no anticipation.

chapters.title: Two Benchmarks
chapters.summary:
Two benchmark data sets test the methods of the book. On the 401(k) data, DML and the horseshoe report one effect for everyone and put it near the same range, well above least squares with nine covariates. The posterior adds what that single number hides: effects that rise with income and an effect on the untreated that differs from the effect on the treated. A Bayesian causal forest did not converge on these data, so the chapter reports no forest estimates and the income profile still lacks a check by a second model class. Overlap is adequate but thin at low incomes. On the LaLonde benchmark the randomized experiment gives a benchmark effect, the raw difference with survey controls is badly off, and flexible methods land much closer. The chapter reports the numbers with their posteriors, discusses overlap and the outcome distribution, and says where the methods still differ.

chapters.title: Two Applications in Health
chapters.summary:
Two health applications close the applied chapters. The first estimates the effect of quitting smoking on weight gain over eleven years in the NHEFS cohort. Three Bayesian models agree with each other and with the published analysis, and a causal forest shows little heterogeneity by smoking intensity or age. chapters.title: A Workflow for Applied Bayesian Causal Inference

chapters.title: Causal Decisions
chapters.summary:
A causal decision maximizes expected utility under an intervention, and the posterior does the averaging, so the Bayes action depends on the whole posterior and not only on the average effect. This chapter separates evidential from causal expected utility and treats policy evaluation, structural estimation and the Lucas critique, games and strategic interaction, industrial organization, mechanism design, targeting and cost effectiveness, climate and fiscal policy, and behavioural departures. A result bounds the regret of the Bayes policy by the posterior's expected error. The chapter ends with risk sensitive decisions computed from a posterior. The chapter is mostly a map of where posterior based decisions differ from decisions based on one estimate, with worked examples and exercises.

chapters.title: The Causal Effect of a Merger
chapters.summary:
A merger is a treatment applied once, to one industry, and never at random, so its price effect can only come from a model. This chapter defines the merger as the intervention do(H := H post) on the form of competition and shows that, under modularity and given the premerger data, the price effect depends on three nonlinear demand parameters and the form of competition alone. The agency's answer is then a pushforward posterior. Markups are the hinge: the Lerner index, upward pricing pressure and the merger price effect follow from the markup map. The chapter explains why orthogonal moments fall short for a nonlinear fixed point, then learns the posterior of the estimands and of conduct by simulating industries and training a network on summary statistics. Calibration on fresh industries compares the posterior with the usual BLP moment estimator, and a section covers wrong conduct.

#### From the literature

The chapter presents or builds on the random coefficients logit demand model (Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes 1995), merger simulation and upward pricing pressure (Nevo 2000; Farrell and Shapiro 2010; Miller and Weinberg 2017), Bayesian estimation of BLP models (Viard, Gron and Polson 2015), approximate Bayesian computation with summary statistics (Frazier, Martin, Robert and Rousseau 2018).

#### New results

- [Identification of the merger effect](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#merger_effect_depends_only_on_demand_and_conduct) (Proposition 20.5, page 399; proved): Given the premerger data, the price effect of a merger is a function of the nonlinear demand parameters and the form of competition alone, so the agency question is a question about their posterior. New in this book.
- [Falsifying a conduct model](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#falsifying_a_conduct_model_under_logit) (Proposition 20.7, page 400; proved): Under logit demand a candidate form of competition is rejected by the instruments unless its markup function differs from the truth only by a combination of cost shifters. New in this book.
- [First order flatness at zero heterogeneity](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#first_order_flatness_at_zero_heterogeneity) (Proposition 20.11, page 401; proved): At zero taste heterogeneity the market shares of the random coefficients logit are flat to first order in the heterogeneity scale, so moments built on shares carry no first order information about it. New in this book.
- [Markup pressure versus GUPPI under logit](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#markup_pressure_exceeds_guppi_under_logit) (Lemma 20.13, page 402; proved): Under logit demand and Bertrand Nash pricing the exact markup increase from a merger exceeds the gross upward pricing pressure index whenever the merger partner has a positive share. New in this book.
- [A Bayes rule for merger review](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#bayes_rule_for_merger_review) (Proposition 20.15, page 404; proved): The agency should challenge a merger when the posterior probability of harm exceeds a ratio of the two error costs, or, for graded costs, when expected excess harm outweighs the cost of blocking. New in this book.
- [Model averaging over conduct](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_causality_book/results.html#model_averaging_over_conduct_variance) (Proposition 20.16, page 404; proved): The posterior variance of a merger estimand splits into a within conduct term and a between conduct term, and a procedure that fixes one conduct omits the second. chapters.title: Open Problems
chapters.summary:
This chapter lists twenty problems that earlier chapters raise and leave open. Each is stated as a setting, what is known, and a conjecture or an open question. results.name: Range of the average effect under a stable odds ratio
results.summary: With one conditional odds ratio e^psi for every unit, the average risk difference over all possible case mixes fills the interval from 0 to tanh(psi/4), so the same stable effect supports very different averages.
results.statement: Let $\psi>0$, let $\gamma$ be the baseline log odds of a unit, with probability law $Q$ over $\gamma$, and let every unit have the logit model $\operatorname{logit}\mathbb{P}(Y=1)=\gamma+\psi t$ for treatment $t\in\{0,1\}$. Write $\tau_Q(\psi)=\mathbb{E}_Q\{\operatorname{expit}(\gamma+\psi)-\operatorname{expit}(\gamma)\}$ for the average effect on the risk difference scale. Then, as $Q$ ranges over all probability laws on $\gamma$, $\{\tau_Q(\psi):Q\}=(0,\tanh(\psi/4)]$, and the supremum is attained only by the point mass at $\gamma=-\psi/2$. Equivalently, an average effect $\tau\in(0,1)$ is generated by the odds ratio $e^{\psi}$ under some case mix if and only if $\psi\ge4\operatorname{artanh}(\tau)$.
results.label: gr:prop:range

results.name: Separability
results.summary: The expectation of a function of two potential outcomes is determined by the two arm laws alone exactly when that function is a sum of a function of each outcome.
results.statement: Let the outcome space $\mathcal Y$ be finite, let $f:\mathcal Y\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb{R}$, and let $\mathcal F(F_1,F_0)$ be the Fr\'echet class of joint laws on $\mathcal Y\times\mathcal Y$ with margins $F_1$ and $F_0$. The following are equivalent. (i) $f$ is separable: $f(a,b)=\alpha(a)+\beta(b)$ for some $\alpha,\beta:\mathcal Y\to\mathbb{R}$. (ii) $\int f\,dF$ is constant on $\mathcal F(F_1,F_0)$ for every pair of margins. (iii) $\int f\,dF$ is constant on $\mathcal F(F_1,F_0)$ for one pair of margins with full support.
results.label: gr:thm:sep

results.name: Identified estimands are functions of the margins
results.summary: Any functional of the potential outcome distribution that an experiment identifies depends on the data only through the two arm laws.
results.statement: Let $\Psi$ be any functional, linear or not, of the joint law $F$ of the two potential outcomes of a unit drawn from the urn, with margins $(F_1,F_0)$. If $\Psi$ is identified from every design that reveals the margins, that is, if $\Psi(F)=\Psi(F')$ whenever $F$ and $F'$ have the same margins, then $\Psi$ is a function of $(F_1,F_0)$.
results.label: gr:cor:complete

results.name: Stratified urns and the reversal
results.summary: In a stratified randomized experiment the collapsed contrast of arm means is unbiased for the finite population effect for every urn if and only if both arms are allocated in proportion to the stratum sizes.
results.statement: Let the units fall into strata $x$ of sizes $n_x$ with $n=\sum_x n_x$. Let the assignment draw $n_{x,1}$ units of stratum $x$ into treatment and the remaining $n_{x,0}$ into control, uniformly at random, with $n_t=\sum_x n_{x,t}$, and let $\bar Y_{x,t}$ be the mean response of arm $t$ in stratum $x$. Then the finite population effect satisfies $\tau_{\mathrm{fp}}=\sum_x (n_x/n)\,\tau_{\mathrm{fp},x}$, and the collapsed contrast $\sum_x (n_{x,1}/n_1)\bar Y_{x,1}-\sum_x (n_{x,0}/n_0)\bar Y_{x,0}$ is unbiased for $\tau_{\mathrm{fp}}$ for every set of potential outcomes if and only if $n_{x,1}/n_1=n_{x,0}/n_0=n_x/n$ for all $x$, that is, if both arms are allocated in proportion to the stratum sizes.
results.label: gr:prop:strat

results.name: The posterior selects the group
results.summary: The log posterior odds of one effect scale against another, or against the saturated model, move linearly in n at a rate equal to the difference of their information gaps, with a log n term for the difference in the number of parameters.
results.statement: Let $\mathcal G$ be a finite collection of groups acting on the baseline space, together with the saturated (heterogeneous) model, each with positive prior probability, a smooth positive prior density on its $d_G$ parameters and a unique interior projection of the true cell laws $F^{\circ}$, at which the Kullback and Leibler divergence has a nonsingular Hessian in those parameters. Let cell $(x,t)$ receive $nw_{x,t}$ independent draws from $F^{\circ}_{x,t}$, and let $D_G=\mathrm{KL}_w(F^{\circ}\,\|\,\mathcal S_G)$ be the weighted divergence from $F^{\circ}$ to the stability class $\mathcal S_G$ of $G$. Then almost surely $\frac1n\log\{\Pi(\mathcal S_G\mid\text{data})/\Pi(\mathcal S_H\mid\text{data})\}\to D_H-D_G$. More precisely, the log posterior odds equal $n(D_H-D_G)-\tfrac12(d_G-d_H)\log n+O_p(\sqrt n)$, and the fluctuation is $O_p(1)$ when both models contain $F^{\circ}$.
results.label: gr:thm:select

results.name: Transport of a stable effect across case mixes
results.summary: The average effect on the scale of a group moves between two case mixes by at most the range of the stratum effects times the total variation distance between the mixes.
results.statement: Let $\psi_G(x)$ be the stratum effect at covariate value $x$ on the scale of a group $G$, with range $R_G=\max_x\psi_G(x)-\min_x\psi_G(x)$, and let $\bar\psi_G(Q)=\sum_x Q_x\psi_G(x)$ be its average over the case mix $Q$. Then for two case mixes $Q$ and $Q'$, $|\bar\psi_G(Q')-\bar\psi_G(Q)|\le R_G\,\|Q-Q'\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le R_G\sqrt{\tfrac12\mathrm{KL}(Q'\,\|\,Q)}$. If the data are exactly stable on $G$, then $R_G=0$ and the effect transports without change on that scale.
results.label: gr:prop:dv

results.statement: Work in the partially linear model $Y=\tau T+g(X)+\varepsilon$, $T=m(X)+\nu$ with fitting errors $\delta_m$ and $\delta_\ell$ of the fitted treatment and outcome regressions, and with $b=\langle\delta_m,\delta_\ell\rangle-\tau\|\delta_m\|^2$ and $J=\mathbb{E}\nu^2$. Let $\hat\tau$ be the pooled cross fitted estimator with folds $I_1,\dots,I_K$ of sizes $n_k$ and fits $\hat\eta^{(-k)}$ that omit $I_k$, and let $b(\hat\eta^{(-k)})$ be the value of $b$ at those fits. Set $\bar\Delta_n=\sum_k(n_k/n)\,b(\hat\eta^{(-k)})\big/\sum_k(n_k/n)\{J+\|\delta_m^{(k)}\|^2\}$ and $U_n=\hat\tau-\tau-\bar\Delta_n$. If $\hat\tau$ and $\bar\Delta_n$ are square integrable (the second holds when $\|\delta_m\|+\|\delta_\ell\|\le1$ for every fit, since then $|\bar\Delta_n|\le\max(1,|\tau|)/J$), then $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\tau)=\operatorname{Var}(\bar\Delta_n)+2\operatorname{Cov}(\bar\Delta_n,U_n)+\operatorname{Var}(U_n)$.

results.name: Identification of the merger effect
results.summary: Given the premerger data, the price effect of a merger is a function of the nonlinear demand parameters and the form of competition alone, so the agency question is a question about their posterior.
results.statement: Consider a market with potential prices $\bm p_t(H)$ under each form of competition $H$, and assume modularity: the intervention $\mathrm{do}(H:=H^{\mathrm{post}})$ replaces $H$ in the equilibrium equation of the structural model and leaves the other structural equations, the parameters $(\beta,\gamma,\theta_2)$ and the exogenous variables unchanged. If the pricing game with post merger conduct $H^{\mathrm{post}}$ has a unique equilibrium (or the equilibrium map applies a fixed selection rule), then the potential prices $\bm p_t(H^{\mathrm{post}})$, and hence the price changes $\Delta\bm p_t=\bm p_t(H^{\mathrm{post}})-\bm p_t$, are functions of the nonlinear demand parameters $\theta_2$, the premerger conduct $H$ and the observed data $(\bm s_t,\bm p_t,\bm x_t)$ alone.
results.label: blp:prop:ident

results.name: Falsifying a conduct model
results.summary: Under logit demand a candidate form of competition is rejected by the instruments unless its markup function differs from the truth only by a combination of cost shifters.
results.statement: Under logit demand with price coefficient $\alpha$, price satisfies $p_{jt}=\bm w_{jt}^\top\gamma+g_{H^\star}(\bm s_t)_j/\alpha+\omega_{jt}$, where $H^\star$ is the true conduct, $\bm s_t$ the vector of market shares, $\bm w_{jt}$ cost shifters and $g_H$ the known markup function of conduct $H$ in the shares. Let $\bm z_{jt}$ be instruments with $\mathbb{E}[\omega_{jt}\mid\bm z_{jt}]=0$, where $\bm w_{jt}$ is a function of $\bm z_{jt}$. A candidate $H$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[p_{jt}-\bm w_{jt}^\top\gamma'-g_H(\bm s_t)_j/\alpha'\mid\bm z_{jt}]=0$ for some $(\gamma',\alpha')$ if and only if there are $\alpha'$ and $\bm\gamma_\Delta$ with $\mathbb{E}[g_{H^\star}(\bm s_t)_j/\alpha-g_H(\bm s_t)_j/\alpha'\mid\bm z_{jt}]=\bm w_{jt}^\top\bm\gamma_\Delta$ almost surely.
results.label: blp:prop:conduct

results.name: First order flatness at zero heterogeneity
results.summary: At zero taste heterogeneity the market shares of the random coefficients logit are flat to first order in the heterogeneity scale, so moments built on shares carry no first order information about it.
results.statement: Let consumer $i$ have utility $V_{ij}=\delta_j+\sigma\eta_i\zeta_j$ for product $j$, with $\eta_i$ independent of the other draws, $\mathbb{E}\eta_i=0$, $\mathbb{E}\eta_i^2=1$, and $\zeta_j$ a product characteristic, with an outside good $j=0$ having $\zeta_0=0$. Write $s^0_j$ for the logit shares at $\sigma=0$ and $\bar\zeta=\sum_{k=0}^Js^0_k\zeta_k$. Then at $\sigma=0$, $\partial s_j/\partial\sigma=0$ and $\partial^2s_j/\partial\sigma^2=s^0_j\{(\zeta_j-\bar\zeta)^2-\sum_{k=0}^Js^0_k(\zeta_k-\bar\zeta)^2\}$, and the inverted mean utilities satisfy $\delta(\sigma)=\delta(0)+\tfrac12\sigma^2\bm a+o(\sigma^2)$ with $\bm a=-(\partial\bm s/\partial\delta)^{-1}\partial^2\bm s/\partial\sigma^2$.
results.label: blp:prop:flat

results.name: Markup pressure versus GUPPI under logit
results.summary: Under logit demand and Bertrand Nash pricing the exact markup increase from a merger exceeds the gross upward pricing pressure index whenever the merger partner has a positive share.
results.statement: Under logit demand with price coefficient $\alpha$ and premerger Bertrand Nash pricing, let firms $f$ and $n$ merge, with total shares $s_f$ and $s_n$, and let $s_j$ be the share of product $j$ and $p_j$ its price. For a product $j$ of firm $f$, the change in the optimal markup at premerger prices is $\Delta m_j=s_n/\{\alpha(1-s_f)(1-s_f-s_n)\}$ and $p_j\,\mathrm{GUPPI}_j=s_n/\{\alpha(1-s_j)(1-s_n)\}$, where GUPPI is the gross upward pricing pressure index, so $\Delta m_j>p_j\,\mathrm{GUPPI}_j$ whenever $s_n>0$, with equality if and only if $s_n=0$. Products of nonmerging firms have $\Delta m_k=0$.
results.label: blp:lem:pressure

results.name: A Bayes rule for merger review
results.summary: The agency should challenge a merger when the posterior probability of harm exceeds a ratio of the two error costs, or, for graded costs, when expected excess harm outweighs the cost of blocking.
results.statement: Let $\Delta p/p$ be the merging parties' price effect (the mean, over their products and over markets, of the proportional price change $(p^\ast_{jt}-p_{jt})/p_{jt}$) and $r$ a harm threshold. If challenging a benign merger ($\Delta p/p\le r$) costs $\ell_1$ and clearing a harmful one ($\Delta p/p>r$) costs $\ell_2$, the Bayes rule challenges if and only if $\mathbb{P}(\Delta p/p>r\mid\mathrm{data})>\ell_1/(\ell_1+\ell_2)$. If instead clearing costs $\ell_2(\Delta p/p-r)_+$, the rule challenges if and only if $\ell_2\,\mathbb{E}[(\Delta p/p-r)_+\mid\mathrm{data}]>\ell_1\,\mathbb{P}(\Delta p/p\le r\mid\mathrm{data})$.
results.label: blp:prop:decision

results.name: Model averaging over conduct
results.summary: The posterior variance of a merger estimand splits into a within conduct term and a between conduct term, and a procedure that fixes one conduct omits the second.
results.statement: Let $\varpi_H=\mathbb{P}(H\mid\mathrm{data})$ be the posterior probability of conduct $H$, and for an estimand $e$ let $\mu_H=\mathbb{E}[e\mid\mathrm{data},H]$ and $v_H=\operatorname{Var}(e\mid\mathrm{data},H)$. Then $\mathbb{E}[e\mid\mathrm{data}]=\bar\mu=\sum_H\varpi_H\mu_H$ and $\operatorname{Var}(e\mid\mathrm{data})=\sum_H\varpi_Hv_H+\sum_H\varpi_H(\mu_H-\bar\mu)^2$. A procedure that conditions on a single conduct $\hat H$ and reports $\mu_{\hat H}$ has posterior expected squared error $\operatorname{Var}(e\mid\mathrm{data})+(\mu_{\hat H}-\bar\mu)^2$, and its reported variance $v_{\hat H}$ omits the between conduct term.
results.label: blp:prop:bma
